props.title: The Creeping Terror
props.initialSlug: Slow alien slug terrorizes small town, eats locals

sections.content: The Creeping Terror stands as one of the most fascinatingly inept sci-fi horror films ever made, joining the pantheon of "so-bad-they're-good" classics like Plan 9 from Outer Space (1959) and Robot Monster (1953). The film's production history is arguably more entertaining than the movie itself - most of the original audio was allegedly lost, leading to endless narration over silent footage. The "monster" appears to be a carpet-covered contraption with visible human legs shuffling underneath, while victims literally crawl into its mouth during attack scenes.

sections.content: The mid-1960s marked a peculiar era for low-budget science fiction, with regional filmmakers trying to capitalize on the drive-in market. The Creeping Terror shares DNA with films like The Beast of Yucca Flats (1961) and Monster A-Go-Go (1965) - all made on shoestring budgets with amateur actors and questionable technical skills. Director Art J. Nelson (under the pseudonym Vic Savage) allegedly scammed investors and disappeared with much of the film's budget. SUBHEAD: The Legacy of "Bad" Science Fiction

While easy to dismiss as pure schlock, films like The Creeping Terror influenced later intentionally campy productions like The Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975) and modern homages like Lost Skeleton of Cadavra (2001). The film's earnest attempt at serious sci-fi horror despite obvious limitations makes it more endearing than cynical modern "mockbusters" like Sharknado (2013).
